title: Nutrition science: macronutrients, vitamins and minerals
note: Macronutrients (carbohydrate, protein, fat) supply energy and building blocks. Vitamins mostly work as coenzymes or signaling molecules; minerals serve as structure, cofactors and electrolytes. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in the body, while most water-soluble ones are not.

read.title: Vitamins as enzyme helpers
text: Vitamins provide almost no energy themselves, yet without them the body cannot use its fuel. The reason is that many vitamins become coenzymes, small molecules that enzymes need in order to work. Niacin is converted into NAD, which carries electrons in hundreds of energy-releasing reactions. Riboflavin becomes FMN and FAD, which play a similar electron-carrying role. Thiamin becomes thiamin pyrophosphate, a cofactor for enzymes in glucose, amino acid and lipid metabolism.

Other vitamins have narrower jobs. Vitamin K is the coenzyme for an enzyme that carboxylates clotting proteins such as prothrombin, so it is needed for normal clotting. Vitamin C is required to make collagen and helps absorb plant iron. Folate and vitamin B12 support the one-carbon chemistry used to build DNA, which is why a shortage of either shows up first in rapidly dividing cells such as red blood cell precursors.

Solubility matters too. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) are absorbed with dietary fat and stored in the liver and fatty tissue, so they can accumulate. Most water-soluble vitamins are not stored in large amounts, with B12 an important exception.
